---
title: "Exposure offsets"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

A count is inseparable from its opportunity window. The [Poisson-regression page](poisson-regression.qmd) introduces the count family and log link. For Nettle's country data, area is a proposed exposure: larger countries provide more geographic space in which languages are counted. An **offset** fixes the exposure coefficient rather than estimating it.

This page first derives the offset from a rate model, then fits the resulting count mean and checks how the fixed exposure term changes coefficient interpretation.

```{r}
#| label: load-nettle-offset
#| echo: true
path <- "data/nettle/nettle-1999-climate.csv"
if (file.exists(path)) {
  nettle <- read.csv(path)
} else {
  url <- paste0("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodowinter/",
                "applied_statistics_book_data/master/nettle_1999_climate.csv")
  source_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".csv")
  download.file(url, source_file, mode = "wb")
  stopifnot(digest::digest(source_file, "sha256", file = TRUE, serialize = FALSE) ==
    "3c5abfbec7b2132a9b81ee9a178cbd5559426578032b60c6c4ad74046898793b")
  raw <- read.csv(source_file)
  nettle <- data.frame(country = raw$Country, log10_population = raw$Population,
    log10_area_km2 = raw$Area, log_area_km2 = log(10) * raw$Area,
    mean_growing_season_months = raw$MGS, language_count = as.integer(raw$Langs))
}
stopifnot(nrow(nettle) == 74L)
```

If $A_i$ is area and $r_i$ is the expected language rate per unit area, then

$$
\lambda_i=A_i r_i,
$$

so

$$
\log\lambda_i=\log A_i+\log r_i
=\log A_i+\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{MGS}_i.
$$

The offset is $\log A_i$ with coefficient fixed at one.

That fixed coefficient makes a strong proportionality claim. Holding growing season fixed, two otherwise identical countries with areas $A$ and $2A$ have

$$
\frac{\lambda(2A)}{\lambda(A)}
=\frac{2A\exp(\eta)}{A\exp(\eta)}=2.
$$

An offset model thus says twice the area implies twice the expected language count. A free-area model replaces the fixed one by $\gamma\log A_i$; an ordinary area covariate on the unlogged scale instead assumes $\log\lambda_i$ changes linearly per square kilometer. These are different scientific claims.

```{r}
#| label: derive-and-fit-offset
#| echo: true
nettle$derived_log_area <- log(10) * nettle$log10_area_km2
stopifnot(max(abs(nettle$derived_log_area - nettle$log_area_km2)) < 1e-10)
fit <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + offset(derived_log_area),
           poisson(link = "log"), nettle)
free_area <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + derived_log_area,
                 poisson(link = "log"), nettle)
raw_area <- exp(nettle$derived_log_area)
area_covariate <- glm(language_count ~ mean_growing_season_months + raw_area,
                      poisson(link = "log"), nettle)
nettle$fitted_count <- predict(fit, type = "response")
head(nettle[c("country", "language_count", "fitted_count")])
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-area-specifications
#| echo: true
data.frame(model = c("log-area offset", "estimated log-area coefficient",
                     "raw-area covariate"),
           area_coefficient = c(1, coef(free_area)["derived_log_area"],
                                coef(area_covariate)["raw_area"]))
```

```{r}
#| label: offset-count-plot
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(nettle, aes(language_count, fitted_count)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "grey65", linewidth = .5) +
  geom_point(size = 1.5, color = "#1F5A85") +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Observed language count", y = "Fitted language count") +
  theme_classic()
```

The source `Area` column is base-10 logarithmic. A Poisson log link uses natural logarithms, hence the explicit conversion $\log A_i=\log(10)\log_{10}A_i$. Treating area as exposure assumes proportionality between expected count and area. Nettle's paper estimates the area coefficient, so this fixed-one version is a teaching model rather than a reproduced analysis.

Changing area units does not change the rate ratio for growing season: multiplying every $A_i$ by a constant adds that constant's logarithm to the offset and shifts the intercept. But using `log10(A)` without multiplying by $\log(10)$ changes the fixed exposure coefficient and hence changes the model.

## Recap and check

1. Is “twice the area means twice the expected languages” scientifically defensible here? It is the offset model's assumption, not a fact supplied by the data; comparing the estimated area coefficient makes that assumption inspectable.
2. Why must the offset use natural logs? `glm(..., family = poisson(link = "log"))` uses the natural-log linear predictor.

The [worked Poisson analysis](poisson-regression-example.qmd) carries the offset model through interpretation and model criticism.
